items.title: L10: A decision framework for strategic judgement questions
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Making Effective Decisions, Seeing the Big Picture; HM Treasury Green Book and Magenta Book
items.body: At senior interviews, questions often present a trade-off with no right answer: 'You have budget for one of three programmes; how do you choose?'. The panel is scoring the quality of your reasoning, not the option you pick. A reliable framework has six parts. First, clarify the objective and constraints: what is the decision for, who decides, by when, and what must not be compromised, such as legal duties or safety. Second, set the criteria before comparing options, for instance impact on users, cost, deliverability, risk and fit with priorities, and say how you would weigh them. Naming criteria first protects you from picking a favourite and then justifying it afterwards. Third, generate and compare options, including doing nothing or doing less, which the government's appraisal guidance in the Green Book treats as a necessary baseline. Fourth, test the evidence: what do you know, what are you assuming, and what could you find out quickly? Fifth, recommend, with the main risk and how you would reduce it. Sixth, say how you would review the decision: what you would monitor, when you would revisit it and what would make you change course. This last step shows that you treat decisions as reversible hypotheses where possible. Throughout, state assumptions out loud and be willing to say what extra information would change your recommendation. Avoid two traps: refusing to commit ('it depends') and committing instantly without reasoning. Panels also listen for who you would consult, because good judgement includes knowing which expertise you lack. The Magenta Book's emphasis on evaluation supports the final step: build in learning from the start.

questions.prompt: In the framework, which step should come before comparing the options?

options.text: Asking the panel which option they like
Choosing your preferred option
Setting the criteria and how you would weigh them
Describing the risks of the cheapest option

questions.hint: Criteria first prevents justifying a favourite afterwards.

questions.prompt: Why does the Green Book treat 'do nothing' or 'do less' as an option?

options.text: It is required to be the final recommendation whenever the evidence is uncertain
It provides a baseline against which other options are judged
It shows that the decision is not important enough to justify spending money
It is the cheapest option and so is usually the one finally chosen by the department

questions.hint: A baseline is needed to show the value of acting.

questions.prompt: A panel asks how you would choose between three programmes. What is the panel mainly scoring?

options.text: The quality of your reasoning rather than the option you pick
Whether you pick the option the panel members would themselves prefer
How quickly you reach a firm answer without needing more information
Whether you pick the cheapest of the three programmes on offer

questions.hint: There is rarely a single right answer.

questions.prompt: Which response shows the weakness of refusing to commit?

options.text: 'I would recommend option B, mainly because of deliverability, and review it in six months.'
'I would choose A, unless the user data shows demand is lower than assumed.'
'On the evidence so far I lean to option A, but I would test one assumption first.'
'It depends on a lot of things, so I would need to see more before saying anything.'

questions.hint: A recommendation with caveats is expected.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the final step, saying how you would review the decision?

options.text: It shows decisions are treated as hypotheses to be monitored and changed if needed
It shows you are likely to change your mind often and cannot hold to a view
It replaces the need to set criteria, because the review will correct any error
It lets you avoid making a firm recommendation, since the decision can be revisited later

questions.prompt: Which statement best shows stating assumptions?

options.text: 'Demand will definitely stay level, so I have based the whole plan on that.'
'I will not need to assume anything here, as the facts are all in front of me.'
'I am assuming demand stays level; if it doubled, I would favour option C.'
'The figures are what they are, and I would work with them as they stand.'

questions.prompt: What does 'who you would consult' add to a judgement answer?

options.text: It lengthens the answer harmlessly, which gives the panel more to score
It moves responsibility for the outcome onto the people you consult
It shows you cannot decide alone and need others to take the decision
It shows you recognise the limits of your own expertise

questions.prompt: Which is the trap of committing instantly?

options.text: Describing the risks too early, before the options have been set out
Choosing an option with no reasoning, which panels cannot score
Showing too much confidence for the grade, which panels mark down
Naming the criteria in the wrong order, so the weighting is unclear

questions.prompt: What does the first step of clarifying the objective and constraints include?

options.text: Which option the department already prefers and how to justify it afterwards
Who decides, by when, and what must not be compromised such as legal duties
How the decision would be reported in the press and by whom
The history of earlier programmes of this type and why each one closed

questions.prompt: Which element does the Magenta Book's emphasis on evaluation support in this framework?

options.text: Building in learning and review from the start
Choosing the cheapest option
Setting criteria after comparing options
Ignoring uncertain evidence

items.title: L10: Public money, propriety and ministerial direction
items.source: HM Treasury, Managing Public Money; Civil Service Code; Ministerial Code
items.body: Senior interviews may test whether you understand the framework in which public money is spent. HM Treasury's Managing Public Money sets out four standards used to assess a spending proposal. Regularity: spending must be within the authority given by Parliament and comply with the relevant rules. Propriety: it must meet standards of conduct, fairness and avoid personal gain or favouritism. Value for money: it should make good use of resources to achieve the intended outcomes. Feasibility: it must be capable of being delivered successfully. In each department the Permanent Secretary is normally the Accounting Officer, personally accountable to Parliament for the stewardship of the department's resources. If a minister proposes a course of action that the Accounting Officer thinks would breach regularity or propriety, or be a poor use of money or not feasible, the Accounting Officer sets out the concern in advice. If the minister still wishes to proceed, the Accounting Officer can ask for a written instruction, called a ministerial direction. This keeps responsibility clear and is exceptional. A strong interview answer shows proportion. If you were a senior leader in a team whose minister asked for something you thought poor value, you would give clear, evidence-based advice, set out the risks, escalate through your line to the Accounting Officer if unresolved, and then, if the decision is lawful and properly directed, implement it. You would not refuse openly, mislead the minister or quietly work against the decision. You would also keep an accurate record of advice given. Avoid claiming powers you do not hold. Describe your role in the chain: advising, escalating, implementing.

questions.prompt: Which are the four standards in Managing Public Money?

options.text: Legality, loyalty, efficiency and accuracy
Transparency, risk, impact and delivery
Regularity, propriety, value for money and feasibility
Honesty, speed, cost and quality

questions.prompt: What does regularity mean?

options.text: Spending takes place on a regular timetable that is agreed with the department
Spending is approved by the minister, who accepts personal responsibility for the sum
Spending is reviewed each year by the minister and approved again for the next year
Spending is within the authority given by Parliament and complies with the rules

questions.hint: It concerns legal and parliamentary authority.

questions.prompt: Who is normally the Accounting Officer of a department?

options.text: The head of finance
The Prime Minister
The Secretary of State
The Permanent Secretary

questions.hint: The Permanent Secretary is personally accountable to Parliament.

questions.prompt: What is a ministerial direction?

options.text: A request by a minister to the department to review an existing policy before a decision
A written instruction from a minister to proceed after an Accounting Officer has raised concerns
A department's annual spending plan, agreed with the Treasury before the financial year
A minister's public statement explaining why a department has decided to spend money

questions.prompt: A minister wants to proceed with a course of action you think is poor value. What should a senior leader do first?

options.text: Give clear, evidence-based advice setting out the risks
Leak the concern to the media so that the public can decide
Quietly delay the work so that the decision is overtaken by events
Refuse openly to work on it until the minister has changed their mind

questions.prompt: If advice is not accepted and the decision is lawful and properly directed, what is the expected next step?

options.text: Ignore it and carry on with other work until it is withdrawn
Work against it quietly, since you disagreed with the decision
Implement it, keeping a record of the advice given
Resign publicly to show that you cannot support the decision

questions.hint: Implement lawful decisions of the government.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would breach propriety?

options.text: Choosing the lowest-cost bid that meets every requirement in the published specification
Awarding work to a supplier because a friend runs it
Publishing the criteria for an award before bids are received from suppliers
Documenting the reasons for a decision so that it can be reviewed later by auditors

questions.hint: Propriety covers fairness and avoiding personal gain.

questions.prompt: What does 'feasibility' ask?

options.text: Whether the proposal is capable of being delivered successfully
Whether the proposal is cheap enough to fit within the existing budget
Whether the proposal is popular with the public and likely to win support
Whether the proposal was approved in a previous year by the same minister

questions.prompt: Why is a ministerial direction described as exceptional?

options.text: They are only used for very small sums of money
They are issued every year for each department as a matter of routine
Accounting Officers normally resolve concerns through advice before it is needed
Ministers are not allowed to issue them except in a national emergency

questions.hint: It is a last resort for serious concerns.

questions.prompt: Which answer shows proportion in a senior interview?

options.text: Say it is not your job to advise ministers at all, only to carry out their decisions
Say the minister must be overruled by the department, whatever the minister has decided
Claim authority to block the decision if you think it unwise, and say so publicly to the press
Describe your role as advising, escalating and implementing, without claiming powers you do not hold

items.title: L10: Equality, fairness and the Public Sector Equality Duty
items.source: Equality Act 2010, section 149; Civil Service Code; GOV.UK guidance on the Public Sector Equality Duty
items.body: Leaders in the Civil Service are expected to understand the Public Sector Equality Duty, set out in section 149 of the Equality Act 2010. When exercising their functions, public bodies must have due regard to three aims: eliminate unlawful discrimination, harassment and victimisation; advance equality of opportunity between people who share a protected characteristic and those who do not; and foster good relations between them. The protected characteristics are age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. 'Due regard' means that equality must be consciously considered when developing policies or making decisions, with evidence, and early enough to influence the outcome; it does not guarantee a particular result. In practice, departments assess the impact of proposals on different groups, consult affected people, and record how the analysis informed the decision. A strong interview answer on inclusion avoids slogans and gives specific action. For example, a leader noticed that part-time staff were missing development opportunities, looked at the data, changed how opportunities were advertised and tracked take-up. It also shows impartiality: treating people fairly while recognising that equal treatment may require different support, such as an adjustment for a disabled colleague. Be careful not to stereotype or make assumptions about groups. If you describe inclusion in recruitment, mention structured questions, diverse panels, and challenging bias when it appears. Panels will also listen for how you handle a team member raising a complaint about discrimination: take it seriously, follow the policy, protect from victimisation and keep matters confidential.

questions.prompt: Where is the Public Sector Equality Duty set out?

options.text: In the Official Secrets Act
In section 149 of the Equality Act 2010
In the Freedom of Information Act 2000
In the Civil Service Code only

questions.hint: It is a statutory duty on public bodies.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the three aims of the duty?

options.text: Advance equality of opportunity
Promote the government's policies
Guarantee equal outcomes
Reduce staffing costs

questions.hint: The three aims are elimination, advancing equality, fostering good relations.

questions.prompt: Which is a protected characteristic?

options.text: Height
Political preference
Educational attainment
Pregnancy and maternity

questions.prompt: What does 'due regard' require?

options.text: A report written after a decision to explain why equality was not affected
A legal challenge to every policy that could affect any group of people
Conscious consideration of equality, with evidence, early enough to influence the decision
A guarantee of a particular result for people who share a protected characteristic

questions.prompt: What does a department typically do to show due regard?

options.text: Avoid collecting data on groups so that no one can be accused of bias
Delay all decisions until every group has been consulted at length
Publish a statement of values on its website and ask staff to sign up to it
Assess the impact on different groups and record how it informed the decision

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest answer on inclusion?

options.text: 'I have never had any complaints about fairness in my time as a manager, and I check regularly.'
'I believe strongly in inclusion and I treat every member of my team in exactly the same way, always.'
'Part-time staff were missing development; I checked the data, changed how opportunities were advertised and tracked take-up.'
'Our team is already very diverse, so I have not needed to take any specific action on inclusion.'

questions.prompt: Why might equal treatment require different support?

options.text: Because equality means identical outcomes
Some people need adjustments to have the same opportunity
Because different people prefer different treatment
Because the law demands preferential treatment

questions.prompt: What should you avoid in an inclusion answer?

options.text: Stereotyping or making assumptions about groups
Consulting those affected before you decide what to do about it
Using data about different groups of staff when you describe the problem
Giving a specific example with a result at the end of your answer

questions.prompt: A team member complains of discrimination. What is the best leadership response?

options.text: Take it seriously, follow the policy, protect from victimisation and keep matters confidential
Talk to the person accused first, without making a record, to hear their side
Wait to see whether the behaviour recurs before you take any action
Tell them to try to resolve it themselves with the colleague, as most issues are minor

questions.prompt: Which recruitment practice supports fairness?

options.text: Questions tailored to each candidate, based on what the panel knows of them
Scoring based on the first impressions the panel formed in the room
Panels chosen from friends of the hiring manager, who know the role well
Structured questions scored against criteria, with trained panels

items.title: L10: Questions that span two behaviours
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: Senior questions often combine behaviours: 'Tell us about a time you had to deliver quickly without compromising quality', or 'a time you changed direction and brought others with you'. The panel will score both. A common mistake is to answer one half in detail and treat the other as an afterthought. A sound approach is to treat the tension between the two behaviours as the heart of the story. First, identify the pair: Delivering at Pace and Managing a Quality Service, or Changing and Improving and Communicating and Influencing. Second, choose an example where the two truly conflicted, for example a deadline that tempted shortcuts, or a change that colleagues resisted. Third, show your reasoning at the point of tension: what you weighed, what you decided and why. Fourth, give evidence for each side separately in the result: the deadline met and the error rate, or the change implemented and the level of buy-in. This ensures each behaviour has its own evidence. It also helps to flag the structure aloud: 'There were two challenges: the timeline and the standard we needed to hold'. Where the question is 'balance', show how you monitored both, for example with a check on a sample of outputs while the deadline approached. If you are not given a pair but suspect the panel is looking for two things, include a short sentence on each. Avoid bolting a second behaviour on at the end with a weak sentence ('and I also communicated well'). Instead, weave actions for both through the story. Finally, use the grade's descriptors for each: the level of scope may differ between behaviours, and your answer should meet it for both.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to treat a two-behaviour question?

options.text: Tell two separate unrelated stories
Answer one behaviour fully and mention the other briefly
Make the tension between the two behaviours the heart of the story
Pick whichever behaviour you prefer

questions.prompt: Which pair does 'deliver quickly without compromising quality' point to?

options.text: Leadership and Seeing the Big Picture
Delivering at Pace and Managing a Quality Service
Changing and Improving and Making Effective Decisions
Working Together and Developing Self and Others

questions.prompt: What should you show at the point of tension?

options.text: Only how you felt about the decision at the time and afterwards
Only what you decided and the date on which it was made
Only who agreed with you and who did not in the team
What you weighed, what you decided and why

questions.prompt: How should the result be presented?

options.text: With a promise to improve both areas the next time you face the choice
With one general sentence that says the work went well and was well received
With separate evidence for each behaviour, such as the deadline met and the error rate
With a list of thanks to the colleagues who helped you in the work

questions.hint: Each behaviour needs its own evidence.

questions.prompt: Which phrase helps signpost the structure?

options.text: 'There were two challenges: the timeline and the standard we needed to hold.'
'There was a great deal going on at the time, so I will pick out some of it.'
'This is a long story, so I will try to keep it as short as I can for you.'
'I am not sure what you are looking for, so tell me if I go wrong.'

questions.prompt: In a 'balance' question, what shows you managed both?

options.text: Lowering the standard slightly so that the deadline could be met on time
Monitoring both, for example checking a sample of outputs as the deadline approached
Asking the manager to decide which of the two should take priority
Working longer hours until both the deadline and the standard were met

questions.prompt: Which is a weak way to cover the second behaviour?

options.text: Weaving actions for both through the story
Naming a decision point for each
Giving a result for each
Adding 'and I also communicated well' at the end

questions.prompt: Why choose an example where the two behaviours genuinely conflicted?

options.text: It is more dramatic, which holds the panel's attention for longer
It avoids probing, because conflict stories are rarely questioned
It lets you show judgement in balancing them
It is shorter, since the story only has to cover one area of work

questions.prompt: How does the grade matter in a two-behaviour answer?

options.text: The scope expected may differ for each, and you should meet it for both
Grade matters only for Leadership, where the descriptors differ most
Only one behaviour is graded, so the other can be treated more lightly
Grade does not matter at senior level, where all examples are treated alike

questions.prompt: You suspect the panel wants two things but the question names one. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore the second behaviour, since the question only names one
Include a short sentence of evidence on each
Ask the panel to confirm what they are looking for before you start
Tell a second story afterwards to be safe, if there is time left

items.title: L10: Partnerships, delivery partners and commercial judgement
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Working Together, Seeing the Big Picture; Government Commercial Function guidance; GOV.UK public procurement guidance
items.body: Much of government delivery depends on others: arm's-length bodies, local authorities, charities, suppliers and other departments. Senior interviews therefore test how you work through partners without direct control. Key principles are clarity, trust and accountability. Clarity means agreeing who does what, by when, to what standard, and how success is measured. Trust is built by honesty about constraints, regular contact and no surprises. Accountability means you remain responsible for outcomes the department has committed to, even when delivery is by someone else, and you need ways of knowing what is happening: shared data, review points and escalation routes. Strong answers describe how you set expectations, how you monitored progress, how you handled problems before they became crises and how you maintained the relationship while holding the partner to account. With suppliers, public procurement must follow the rules and principles of fairness, transparency and value for money. Public contracts are generally awarded through open and fair competition, and conflicts of interest must be declared and managed. Commercial awareness includes understanding what is being bought, how risk is shared, how contract performance is managed and what happens if the supplier fails. Avoid describing partners as obstacles to be managed; panels value respect and shared goals, with candour about conflicting interests. Also be ready to explain how you influence without authority: understanding their incentives, offering something of value, using evidence, building coalitions and escalating only when necessary. When partnerships go wrong, show accountability: what you learned about governance, such as earlier warning indicators or clearer break clauses. Finally, tie the partnership to user outcomes, because that is what ultimately justifies the arrangement.

questions.prompt: Which three principles underpin working through partners?

options.text: Loyalty, seniority and process
Speed, secrecy and control
Clarity, trust and accountability
Cost, volume and speed

questions.hint: These shape how to work without direct control.

questions.prompt: What does clarity with a partner involve?

options.text: Leaving the details to be discovered as the work goes on and everyone learns
Setting expectations only after problems occur, when they are easier to define
Telling them as little as possible so that you keep control over the work
Agreeing who does what, by when, to what standard and how success is measured

questions.prompt: When a partner delivers part of a service, who remains accountable for the outcomes the department has committed to?

options.text: The department
The partner alone, since it carries out the work
The supplier's chief executive, under the contract
Responsibility is shared equally, so each party answers for half

questions.hint: Delegating delivery does not delegate accountability.

questions.prompt: Which supports accountability when a partner delivers?

options.text: Avoiding contact to give them freedom
Shared data, review points and escalation routes
Trust alone
Annual reports only

questions.hint: You need ways to know what is happening.

questions.prompt: Public contracts are generally awarded through what?

options.text: The lowest bid always
Rotation between known suppliers
Direct choice by the minister
Open and fair competition

questions.prompt: Which of these is part of commercial awareness?

options.text: Avoiding written contracts so that arrangements stay flexible for both sides
Knowing the supplier's directors personally so that you can resolve any problems quickly
Understanding how risk is shared and what happens if the supplier fails
Choosing the cheapest contract regardless of how well it manages risk

questions.prompt: Which description of partners will count against you?

options.text: Obstacles to be managed
Bodies that must be held to account
Colleagues with shared goals
Organisations with different incentives

questions.hint: Respect and shared goals are valued.

questions.prompt: How can you influence without authority?

options.text: Threaten escalation early so that the partner understands the stakes
Understand their incentives, offer value, use evidence and build coalitions
Promise whatever the partner asks for to keep them on side
Copy the minister into every email so that they know what is happening

questions.hint: Influence is about understanding and value.

questions.prompt: After a partnership failure, what shows accountability?

options.text: Blaming the partner for failing to deliver what was agreed in the contract
Saying the failure was unavoidable and nobody could have prevented it
Describing what you learned about governance such as earlier warning indicators
Avoiding the topic and moving on to a more successful example

questions.prompt: Why tie a partnership back to user outcomes?

options.text: Because it shortens the answer and leaves time for another question
Because outcomes are what ultimately justify the arrangement
Because it avoids the need to discuss the risks of the arrangement
Because panels like to hear about users and often ask about them

items.title: L10: Prepared-topic exercises with limited preparation time
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance on assessment methods; Civil Service Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing
items.body: Some senior interviews include an exercise in which you receive a brief and a limited preparation time, perhaps thirty to sixty minutes, and then present or discuss with the panel. Common types are a briefing to a senior colleague, a recommendation on a set of options, or a written task followed by questions. The skill is triage under time pressure. In the first few minutes, read the whole brief, note the task, audience, format and word or time limit, and underline the question you must answer. Many candidates lose marks by answering a different question from the one set. Next, scan for facts that matter: figures, dates, constraints, stakeholders and any information that conflicts or is missing. Spot the planted problems: an inconsistent number, a deadline that cannot be met, a stakeholder with a conflicting interest. Decide your recommendation early, even if provisional, because it focuses the reading. Plan the structure on one page: headline recommendation, three reasons, one or two risks, next steps. Allocate your time: a third reading and planning, half building the content, and the rest rehearsing aloud. Practise the opening sentence. If you are unsure of a fact, state your assumption openly. In the discussion, use the brief as evidence, citing facts accurately, and be ready to adjust when panel members introduce new information. Do not try to include everything; selecting what matters is part of the assessment. If you run short of time, finish the structure with a clear conclusion rather than leaving an unfinished section. Finally, keep a calm tone: a steady, organised presentation of a good-enough analysis scores better than a frantic delivery of a complete one.

questions.prompt: What is the first priority when you receive the brief?

options.text: Read the whole brief and note the task, audience, format and limits
Start writing your slides straight away to make best use of the time
Decide how to answer the questions that you expect the panel to ask
Ask the panel for hints about what they would like to see in the answer

questions.prompt: What is a common reason for losing marks?

options.text: Using too few slides for the length of time that the panel has given you
Leaving the preparation room before the time allowed has fully run out
Speaking too slowly, so that the panel cannot cover all the questions
Answering a different question from the one set

questions.prompt: What are 'planted problems'?

options.text: Questions the panel prepares in advance for you to answer at the end of your talk
Extra slides that the panel adds to the presentation after it has started, to test your flexibility
Inconsistencies or constraints in the brief, such as a figure that does not add up or an impossible deadline
Errors in the panel's own notes that you are expected to point out to them during the session

questions.prompt: Why decide your recommendation early?

options.text: It shows the panel your bias before they have asked you anything
It means you do not need to analyse the rest of the brief any more
It prevents any change to your view later, which shows consistency
It focuses the reading and planning, even if provisional

questions.prompt: Which one-page plan structure suits the exercise?

options.text: A timeline of events leading up to the decision, with dates
Headline recommendation, three reasons, one or two risks, and next steps
A list of all the facts in the brief, in the order in which they appear
Background, history and context of the issue, then a short conclusion

questions.prompt: How should preparation time be allocated?

options.text: About a third on reading and planning, half building content, and the rest rehearsing aloud
All of it reading the brief, so that no detail is missed that the panel may ask about
All of it building the content, since the panel marks only what you present on the day
All of it rehearsing aloud, so that the delivery is as smooth and fluent as it can be

questions.prompt: You are unsure about a fact in the brief. What should you do?

options.text: Delay the whole presentation
Invent a fact
Ignore it
State your assumption openly

questions.prompt: A panel member introduces new information during discussion. What is best?

options.text: Take it on board and adjust your recommendation if warranted
Ask the panel member to stop, since you have a plan to follow
Ignore it, as it is outside the brief that you were given
Defend your original recommendation firmly, as changing view looks weak

questions.prompt: Why not try to include everything in the brief?

options.text: The brief is deliberately misleading
Panels dislike detail
Selecting what matters is part of the assessment
There is never time for any facts

questions.prompt: You run short of time. What is best?

options.text: Stop in the middle of a point and tell the panel you have run out of time
Finish the structure with a clear conclusion rather than leaving a section unfinished
Ask the panel for extra time, explaining that the brief was too long
Speak faster so that every point is covered before the time ends

items.title: L10: Contradictory instructions and unlawful requests
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; Ministerial Code
items.body: Senior candidates may be asked: 'What would you do if you were told to do something you believed was wrong?'. The answer depends on what 'wrong' means, and good answers distinguish between categories. The first is a policy you disagree with but which is lawful: here you give advice, state your concerns, and then implement the decision loyally. The second is an instruction you believe is poor value or unlikely to work: you set out the evidence in writing, escalate through your line management, and, in the case of public spending, the Accounting Officer's process applies. The third is an instruction that is unlawful or conflicts with the Civil Service Code, such as misleading Parliament, misusing public funds or acting in a party-political way. Here you must not comply. The Code says to report it; you can raise it with your line manager, the nominated officer or ultimately the Civil Service Commission. Keep factual records and, where appropriate, seek legal advice from the department's lawyers. The fourth is a situation where you are unsure whether the request is improper: clarify before acting, ask a trusted senior colleague or the nominated officer, and avoid assuming bad faith. Tone matters: be calm, factual and proportionate. Do not leak, do not confront in public and do not simply do as you are told. Another test is when two legitimate instructions conflict, such as a minister's priority and a statutory deadline from another body. Show how you would surface the conflict early to both parties, give a clear analysis of options and ask for a decision from the person with authority. Throughout, show that you understand the role: to advise honestly and implement lawfully.

questions.prompt: A lawful policy you disagree with. What does the Civil Service role require?

options.text: Give advice and voice concerns, then implement the decision loyally
Work against it quietly, so that the decision is not fully carried out
Leak your concerns to a journalist who is covering the policy
Refuse to work on it, since you cannot support a policy you disagree with

questions.hint: Impartial service of the government of the day.

questions.prompt: An instruction you believe is poor value but lawful. What is the sound response?

options.text: Take it to the press so that the public can judge for themselves whether it is good value
Set out the evidence in writing and escalate through your line, using the Accounting Officer process for spending
Ignore the instruction and carry on with your normal work, since a wasteful instruction cannot be lawful
Comply silently and keep your concerns to yourself, so as not to cause a dispute with senior staff

questions.prompt: You are asked to mislead Parliament. What must you do?

options.text: Pass the task to a junior colleague so that you are not responsible for it
Comply, to avoid conflict with a senior person who has asked you
Comply and keep records of the instruction, in case of later questions
Not comply, and report it under the Code

questions.prompt: Where can concerns that conflict with the Code ultimately be raised?

options.text: A political party
The press office
The Civil Service Commission
The department's finance team only

questions.prompt: You are unsure if a request is improper. What should you do?

options.text: Comply without question, because the request has come from someone senior
Clarify before acting and seek advice from a senior colleague or nominated officer
Wait until the work is done and then decide whether it was proper
Assume bad faith and refuse to act until the person has explained themselves

questions.prompt: Which tone is best when challenging a request?

options.text: Sarcastic, so that the person making the request understands your view
Silent and passive, so that nobody can say you caused any trouble
Calm, factual and proportionate
Angry and public, so that others understand the seriousness of the matter

questions.prompt: Which of these should you not do?

options.text: Seek legal advice
Keep factual records
Raise it with the nominated officer
Leak your concerns to the media

questions.prompt: Two legitimate instructions conflict. What is the best approach?

options.text: Surface the conflict early to both parties, analyse the options and ask for a decision from the person with authority
Choose the instruction you prefer and tell the other party after the event, once it is under way
Wait for the conflict to resolve itself before you take any step, as it often does
Do both partially, so that neither party is wholly disappointed by the progress you make

questions.prompt: Why keep records in these situations?

options.text: They protect you from every consequence if a decision is later challenged
They show what advice was given and what was decided
They replace the need to escalate concerns through your line management
They are only needed for finance matters and not for other types of advice

questions.prompt: What does the panel want to see in this question?

options.text: Understanding of the role: to advise honestly and implement lawfully
Willingness to refuse any instruction that you do not agree with
A strong preference for acting on your own views when you think best
Willingness to follow any instruction given by a senior person

items.title: L10: Building a coherent career narrative
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Experience; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: At senior levels, the panel is interested in the story of your career: why you made the choices you did, how your experience builds towards the role and what you want next. A coherent career narrative is not a list of jobs; it is a thread that links them. Start by identifying two or three themes in your work, such as improving services for users, solving operational problems, or developing teams. Then choose the moves that illustrate each theme. For every step, be able to say what you wanted to learn, what you delivered and what it prepared you for. If your career has gaps, changes of direction or sideways moves, explain them briefly and positively: what you learned and why it strengthened your application. Avoid describing leaving a role only in terms of what was wrong with it. A sound opening answer to 'Tell us about yourself' runs for around two minutes: your current role and a headline achievement, one or two earlier steps that built the relevant experience, and why this role is the logical next step. Test the narrative by asking whether a stranger could repeat it in a sentence. Link it to the advert: the essential criteria and behaviours. Be ready to defend decisions that look unusual, such as leaving a promotion route to gain breadth. Keep it honest; panels check details with probes, and inconsistent dates or inflated titles can undermine trust. Update the narrative after every significant project. Finally, make sure it looks forward: panels want to know what you will do in the post, so end by saying what you would bring and what you want to achieve in your first year.

questions.prompt: What is a career narrative?

options.text: A summary of your qualifications and the courses that you have taken
A copy of your CV read aloud with a short comment on each job
A thread linking your roles around themes, not just a list of jobs
A list of jobs in date order, with the dates and grades of each

questions.hint: The panel wants the logic of your choices.

questions.prompt: How should you start building one?

options.text: Choose the most senior title and build the narrative around that one
List every job you have held in date order, so that nothing is left out
Copy the structure of someone else's story who got the same job
Identify two or three themes in your work and choose moves that illustrate them

questions.prompt: For each career step, what should you be able to say?

options.text: What you wanted to learn, what you delivered and what it prepared you for
How long you stayed in each job before you moved on to the next
Who your manager was and what they thought of your work
The salary at each step and how it compared with the one before it

questions.prompt: How should a career gap or sideways move be handled?

options.text: Apologise at length so that the panel knows you recognise the issue
Avoid mentioning it, in case the panel sees it as a weakness
Say that it was irrelevant to the role and should not be discussed
Explain it briefly and positively, with what you learned

questions.prompt: Why avoid describing leaving a role only in terms of what was wrong with it?

options.text: It is against the Code to criticise a former employer
It sounds negative and says little about what you wanted
It shortens the answer, which leaves less time for evidence
It avoids probes, because the panel moves on to a new topic

questions.hint: Focus on what you were moving towards.

questions.prompt: How long should an answer to 'Tell us about yourself' be?

options.text: Around ten minutes
Under thirty seconds
Around two minutes
As long as your CV

questions.prompt: What is a good test of your narrative?

options.text: Whether it uses long words that show your seniority to the panel
Whether it takes longer than a minute to say, which shows its depth
Whether it contains your salary and grade at each stage
Whether a stranger could repeat it in a sentence

questions.prompt: Why must a narrative be honest?

options.text: Panels do not probe senior candidates, so honesty matters less
It is a legal requirement for every application to the Civil Service
Panels check details with probes, and inconsistencies damage trust
It must be short, because long narratives are marked down

questions.prompt: What should the end of the narrative do?

options.text: Look forward to what you would bring and achieve in the role
Repeat your first sentence to give the narrative a neat ending
Apologise for any gaps that you have not explained earlier
List your weaknesses so that the panel is aware of them

questions.prompt: Why link the narrative to the advert?

options.text: To shorten the interview by covering the question in advance
To show how your experience maps to the essential criteria and behaviours
To flatter the department by repeating its own words back to it
To avoid probes, which tend to follow general statements about career

items.title: L10: Thinking aloud and answering under time pressure
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Making Effective Decisions; Civil Service Jobs interview guidance
items.body: Some senior questions give you almost no time: 'A story breaks about your service this morning; what do you do in the next hour?'. The panel is watching how you think. A useful technique is to think aloud in structure. State your priorities first: 'My first aims are to establish the facts, protect those affected and make sure the right people know'. Then sequence actions: gather facts from operational leads, check what has been said publicly, inform your director and the press office, protect users who may be at risk, and agree who speaks. Mention what you would not do: speculate, blame or release information before it is checked. A short pause of five to ten seconds before answering is acceptable and often helps. If you do not know something, say what you would check and from whom. Use time markers ('in the first ten minutes, by midday, by the end of the day') to show you can plan under pressure. Show awareness of roles: press offices, legal teams, senior leaders and ministers' offices have defined responsibilities, and civil servants support ministers who make public statements for government. Remember also the Code: honesty, objectivity and the duty not to mislead. If a panel member interrupts with new facts, adjust calmly: 'That changes my priority; I would now...'. This shows adaptability. After the answer, a one-line summary helps close it. Practise by taking a news item about a public service and answering aloud for ninety seconds, without notes, then reviewing the structure with a friend.

questions.prompt: What is the panel watching in a no-notice scenario?

options.text: How quickly you speak
How you think and structure your response
Whether you avoid pausing
Whether you know the news story

questions.prompt: What is a useful first move when thinking aloud?

options.text: List every possible action in the order in which you think of them
Wait in silence until the panel suggests how you might begin
Ask the panel what happened in the story and who was involved
State your priorities before sequencing actions

questions.prompt: Which action would be unwise in the first hour?

options.text: Releasing information before it has been checked
Informing your director that a story is about to break
Protecting those who may be at risk because of the story
Gathering facts from the operational leads who run the service

questions.prompt: Is a short pause before answering acceptable?

options.text: It must be avoided, because the panel will think that you have no answer
It is forbidden, since panels expect you to answer straight away
A pause of a few seconds is acceptable and often helps
It signals incompetence, so you should always start speaking at once

questions.prompt: Why does using time markers such as 'in the first hour' strengthen an answer to a crisis scenario?

options.text: They show you can plan and sequence actions under pressure
They replace the need to state priorities at the start
They signal that you have rehearsed the exact scenario before
They lengthen the answer so the panel has less time to probe

questions.hint: Sequencing is the skill being tested.

questions.prompt: Who may make public statements for government on a matter?

options.text: Any civil servant
Ministers, supported by civil servants
Only the Permanent Secretary
Only the press office

questions.prompt: A panel member adds new facts mid-answer. What is best?

options.text: Ignore them and keep to the plan you have already set out
Argue that the new facts do not change anything of importance
Adjust calmly and say how your priority changes
Restart your answer from the beginning with the new facts added

questions.prompt: Which Code value is most relevant to public statements?

options.text: Loyalty to the minister, whatever the facts turn out to be
Speed, since the story needs to be answered as soon as possible
Secrecy, since the story is best kept inside the department
Honesty, including not misleading others

questions.prompt: What helps close a short answer?

options.text: A one-line summary of your approach
Asking the panel whether your answer was the one they wanted
Apologising for the lack of detail in what you have said
Repeating the question so that it is clear what you were asked

questions.prompt: What is a good way to practise?

options.text: Read news items silently so that you know what is happening in each public service
Take a news item about a public service and answer aloud for ninety seconds without notes, then review
Memorise model answers to common crisis questions and recite them word for word on the day
Practise only the first line of the answer, which matters more than the rest

items.title: L10: Data, transparency and handling information at senior level
items.source: UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 (ICO guidance); Freedom of Information Act 2000; Civil Service Code
items.body: Senior interviews may include questions touching on information: sharing data across teams, responding to a request for information, or handling a data breach. Key principles help you answer. Under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, organisations processing personal data must follow principles including lawfulness, fairness and transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, and integrity and confidentiality, and must be accountable for compliance. In practice, you use personal data only for the purpose it was collected, hold only what you need and keep it secure. If you suspect a breach that risks people's rights and freedoms, the organisation must normally report it to the Information Commissioner's Office within 72 hours of becoming aware, and tell affected individuals where the risk is high. A strong answer to a breach scenario: contain it, assess the risk, tell your data protection officer and senior leaders at once, record what happened, notify the regulator when required and learn from it. Do not hide or delay. The Freedom of Information Act 2000 gives anyone the right to request information held by public authorities, normally with a response within twenty working days, subject to exemptions such as national security, personal data or commercial interests, some of which need a public interest test. Good practice is to respond helpfully, apply exemptions only where justified and keep records. The Civil Service Code's values apply: honesty means you must not conceal information improperly or mislead. A balanced answer shows that transparency and protection of personal or sensitive data can both be valid and that you take advice from specialists. Avoid sharing data informally, such as through personal email, or making decisions based on information you have not checked for accuracy.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the UK GDPR principles?

options.text: Data maximisation
Data publication
Data minimisation
Data speed

questions.prompt: Within what time must a notifiable breach normally be reported to the ICO?

options.text: 30 days, as for a request for information
7 days
24 hours
72 hours of becoming aware

questions.prompt: Which action is part of a good first response to a breach?

options.text: Wait to see whether anyone notices the breach, so as not to alarm people
Tell no one until the next audit, when it can be dealt with together
Delete the evidence so that it cannot cause further harm
Contain it, assess the risk and tell your data protection officer and senior leaders

questions.prompt: Which law gives people a right to request information held by public authorities?

options.text: The Official Secrets Act
The Freedom of Information Act 2000
The Equality Act 2010
The Data Protection Act alone

questions.prompt: What is the normal time limit for responding to an FOI request?

options.text: Twenty working days
Fifty working days
Two working days
One year

questions.prompt: Which of these may justify withholding information under FOI?

options.text: That it is inconvenient for staff to find and prepare the information
That a manager dislikes the request and the person who made it
An exemption such as personal data or commercial interests
That it is embarrassing for the department if the information is published

questions.prompt: What does purpose limitation mean?

options.text: Sharing data freely between teams so that it is used as widely as possible
Collecting data for any future use that might arise, whether or not it is known
Using data for a purpose chosen later, once the department sees what it holds
Using personal data only for the purpose it was collected

questions.prompt: Why avoid sharing data through personal email?

options.text: It uses more storage than the department allows for each person
It risks security and breaks data protection and information handling rules
It is always forbidden by law in every circumstance, with no exceptions
It is slower than using the departmental system for the same task

questions.prompt: Which Code value applies when answering a request for information?

options.text: Speed, since a quick reply matters more than a complete one
Secrecy, since the information belongs to the department
Honesty: not concealing information improperly or misleading
Loyalty, since information should help your minister before others

questions.prompt: What does a balanced answer show about transparency and data protection?

options.text: That both can be valid and that you take specialist advice
That transparency always wins over every other consideration
That data protection always wins over every other consideration
That the choice between them is arbitrary and depends on mood

items.title: L10: Assessment centres and multi-stage senior selection
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance on assessment methods; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Senior and fast-track competitions often use several stages over days or weeks: online tests, a written exercise, a group or role-play exercise, a presentation and an interview. Each stage is designed to gather different evidence against the Success Profiles elements, so performance in one cannot be assumed to carry over. The assessors usually score each exercise independently, then combine scores in an agreed way, sometimes with a minimum on each stage. Good practice is to prepare for each stage separately. For a group exercise, assessors are typically looking for contribution, listening, building on others' ideas and helping the group to reach a decision, not for dominance. Speaking most is not the same as scoring most. A candidate who invites a quieter member to comment, summarises the discussion and keeps the group to time shows influence and teamwork. In a role-play, for instance a meeting with a difficult stakeholder, assessors look for how you open, listen, test understanding, handle emotion and agree next steps. Written exercises test clarity, accuracy and structure, so plan, answer the question, and check for errors. Between stages, rest and manage energy; fatigue can undermine later performance. Do not discuss exercises in detail with other candidates in ways that breach confidentiality instructions. If you have an adjustment, check that it is in place for each stage. Treat each stage as a fresh start; a poor exercise does not decide the outcome, and strong results elsewhere can offset it. Afterwards, request feedback on each stage to learn where the evidence was strongest.

questions.prompt: Why can performance at one stage not be assumed to carry over?

options.text: Each stage gathers different evidence against the framework
Stages are scored randomly, so past results do not help
Only the last stage matters, whatever has gone before
Stages are repeated until the candidate does well

questions.prompt: What do assessors typically look for in a group exercise?

options.text: Dominating the discussion so that your ideas are heard first
Contribution, listening and helping the group reach a decision
Staying silent to avoid errors that might be noticed
Arguing each point to the end, to show strength of conviction

questions.prompt: Which action shows influence and teamwork in a group exercise?

options.text: Repeating what others have said so that the group knows you agree
Interrupting to make your point before others have finished their own
Staying silent until the discussion is nearly over, then speaking once
Inviting a quieter member to comment and summarising the discussion

questions.prompt: How does speaking for the longest in a group exercise usually affect your score?

options.text: It has no effect, since only the final recommendation is marked
It earns the highest score, because it shows the most initiative
It does not guarantee the highest score, since quality of contribution counts
It earns the lowest score, because dominance is always penalised

questions.prompt: In a role-play with a difficult stakeholder, what do assessors look for?

options.text: Whether you avoid the subject that the stakeholder is upset about
How you open, listen, test understanding, handle emotion and agree next steps
Whether you win the argument with the stakeholder by the end of the meeting
Whether you end the meeting quickly, to show you can manage time

questions.prompt: Which is a feature of a good written exercise?

options.text: Many headings with no conclusion, so that the reader can choose
Length above all, since a longer answer shows more knowledge
Technical jargon, which shows that you understand the field
Clear structure, accuracy and an answer to the question set

questions.prompt: Why manage energy between stages?

options.text: Panels reward candidates who look rested, and mark down those who do not
It shortens the process, as rested candidates finish exercises sooner
Fatigue can undermine later performance
It is a rule of the competition that candidates must take a break between stages

questions.prompt: What should you check for each stage if you have an adjustment?

options.text: That it is in place
That the panel has changed
That others know about it
That it is the same for everyone

questions.prompt: After a poor exercise, what is the sound attitude?

options.text: Ask to repeat it
Assume the outcome is decided
Withdraw
Treat the next stage as a fresh start

questions.prompt: Why request feedback on each stage?

options.text: To avoid applying for similar roles in future
To learn where the evidence was strongest and weakest
To contest the scores of the panel with the evidence you have
To compare your results with those of the other candidates

items.title: L10: Coaching yourself: reflective practice after interviews
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Developing Self and Others; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: Strong candidates treat each interview as data, and build a habit of structured reflection. Straight after an interview, within an hour, write down every question you remember and, for each, jot a few lines of what you said. Memory fades quickly, and the notes are valuable when feedback arrives. Then rate each answer on a simple scale for four things: relevance to the behaviour, personal action, specific result and delivery. This is not about self-criticism; it shows patterns. Note what went well as well as what did not, because strengths need to be repeated deliberately. When feedback arrives, compare it with your own ratings. Where they agree, you have reliable insight. Where the panel scored lower than you expected, your self-view may be over-generous in that area; where they scored higher, you may be underrating yourself. Both are useful calibration. Next, choose one or two changes for the next interview, set a date to practise them, and ask someone to hold you to it. Over time keep a running record of questions asked, stories used and results. If you receive a rejection, allow yourself a short period to process emotions before analysing, because reflection works better when you are calm. Discuss the feedback with a mentor, who can offer an outside view. Reflective practice is also evidence in itself, since it demonstrates Developing Self and Others; you can cite how you used feedback to change your approach. A good example would be: 'After my last interview I noticed I left out results, so I rewrote my examples with figures and practised with a colleague'. This answer proves learning and gives the panel confidence you will keep improving in post.

questions.prompt: When should you note the questions after an interview?

options.text: A week later
Only if you are unsuccessful
Within an hour, while memory is fresh
Never

questions.prompt: Which four things might you rate for each answer?

options.text: Relevance, personal action, specific result and delivery
Length of answer, volume, tone of voice and speed of speech
Humour, confidence, polish and warmth shown to the panel
Dress, posture, eye contact and smile throughout the answer

questions.prompt: Why should reflection after an interview note what went well, as well as what did not?

options.text: Strengths need to be repeated deliberately next time
It avoids a long list of faults that would be hard to act on
It is something panels check when they read your application
It makes the review feel less critical, which reduces nerves

questions.prompt: The panel scored one answer lower than you rated it yourself. What might this suggest?

options.text: The scoring was random and means nothing about your answers
The behaviour is irrelevant to the role and can be ignored
The panel was wrong, and you should ask for the scores to be changed
Your self-view may be over-generous in that area

questions.hint: Compare self-rating with scores to calibrate.

questions.prompt: An answer you rated poorly was scored well by the panel. What might this suggest?

options.text: The panel was lenient and the score will not hold
Your answer was too long and the panel gave credit for effort
You may be underrating yourself in that area
The score was a mistake that will be corrected if you ask

questions.prompt: After feedback, how many changes should you focus on?

options.text: All of them
One or two
None
Twenty

questions.prompt: Why wait briefly before analysing a rejection?

options.text: Panels require a delay
Reflection works better when you are calm
It avoids emotion altogether
Feedback is not available earlier

questions.prompt: What can a mentor add to your reflection?

options.text: A different set of criteria that will be used by your next panel
A guarantee of success at your next interview, once you have talked it through
An outside view of patterns you may miss
The panel's own notes of the interview, which they can request for you

questions.prompt: Why is reflective practice itself useful evidence?

options.text: It avoids probing, because the panel will accept the reflection
It shortens the answer so that you can use time for another topic
It replaces the need for examples, since it shows the same thing
It demonstrates Developing Self and Others

questions.prompt: Which statement best shows learning from feedback?

options.text: 'I noticed I left out results, so I rewrote my examples with figures and practised with a colleague.'
'I did not get the job, but it was fine and I did not mind in the end, as I enjoy my present role.'
'I will try harder next time, and I am sure that it will go better because I want it more.'
'The panel did not understand my examples, so I will explain them more clearly next time.'
